content.title: About
content.content: Eggnog is a traditional festive drink made from eggs, milk, sugar and spirits (usually rum, brandy or whiskey). It has a thick, creamy texture, a sweet‑spicy flavor with hints of vanilla, and the alcohol gives it a warming effect.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggnog originated in medieval England as a "egg punch" and was originally non‑alcoholic.
In the United States the drink became popular during the colonial era, when Caribbean rum was added.
Typical spices for eggnog are cinnamon, nutmeg and clove.
In some regions eggnog is served cold, in others hot, depending on climate and tradition.
There is a non‑alcoholic version often served to children and those who abstain from spirits.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Milk and cream supply calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and dairy contain riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Nutmeg and cinnamon are rich in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Eggnog can trigger allergic reactions in people sensitive to eggs or milk.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional recipes contain a lot of sugar, which may contribute to weight gain and blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Excessive consumption of alcoholic eggnog can lead to intoxication and associated hazards.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: If made with raw eggs and not kept properly chilled, there is a risk of salmonella infection.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve eggnog in small glasses or mugs, often topped with whipped cream and a pinch of nutmeg. It can be enjoyed hot in cold weather or chilled in warm weather. Additional spirits (rum, brandy) may be added to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared eggnog should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion it into sealed containers to prevent oxidation and bacterial growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Hummus is a traditional Middle Eastern dip made from cooked chickpeas, tahini, olive oil, lemon juice, and spices. It has a creamy texture, a mild nutty flavor with a hint of acidity.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hummus has been known in the Arab world for over 700 years.
The word “hummus” comes from Arabic “ḥummuṣ,” meaning “chickpea.”
Tahini (sesame paste) gives hummus its distinctive aroma and boosts its nutritional value.
In the United States, hummus gained popularity in the 1990s and became one of the top-selling vegetarian products by 2020.
There are many variations: roasted red pepper, garlic, olive, avocado, and more.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, making hummus a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil and tahini supply monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Hummus contains folate, iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and vitamin B6.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Chickpeas have a moderate glycemic index, helping to stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Chickpea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes, including chickpeas.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared hummus often contains added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice can aggravate heartburn in people with high stomach acidity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hummus as a dip with vegetable sticks, pita bread, or crackers; use it in sandwiches, wraps, and salads. It can also be blended into sauces or used as a base for vegetarian dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep hummus in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. After opening, cover the surface with plastic wrap to prevent oxidation. Discard if it develops an off smell or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Nuts are edible seeds of various woody plants cultivated in warm regions worldwide. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. Nuts are eaten raw, roasted, or blanched and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and plant‑based milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nuts belong to the Rosaceae family and are related to peaches, plums, and cherries.
There are sweet and bitter varieties; bitter nuts contain toxic compounds and are not sold as regular snacks.
Nut trees have been cultivated for several thousand years.
Nuts are processed into flour, butter, marzipan, and plant milks.
Nut blossoms appear in early spring, before the leaves emerge.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Nuts are one of the best plant sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in nuts is monounsaturated, which can support heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Nuts contribute plant protein and dietary fiber, which promote satiety.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Nuts contain more calcium than most other nuts, benefiting bone health.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Nuts can trigger allergic reactions, which may be severe in some individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Nuts are calorie‑dense, so portion sizes should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole nuts are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Nuts contain oxalates; people prone to kidney stones may need to limit intake. Bitter nuts should never be eaten raw.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Nuts can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, and baked goods, or ground into nut flour and butter. Soaking or blanching softens the skins and makes them easier to remove. Unsalted or lightly salted nuts are a good choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store nuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil rancidity. Discard nuts that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Queso Fresco is a soft, fresh Mexican cheese made from cow’s or goat’s milk. It has a mild, slightly tangy flavor and a creamy, crumbly texture similar to cottage cheese or feta. The cheese is sold in small blocks and is typically eaten fresh.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Queso Fresco is a staple in Mexican cuisine, used in tacos, enchiladas, and salads.
The cheese is not aged, which gives it a high moisture content and soft consistency.
Unlike many hard cheeses, Queso Fresco does not melt; it softens slightly when heated.
In Mexico it is often served with lime, salt, and chili.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Queso Fresco provides a good amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality dairy protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B2 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: Compared with many aged cheeses, Queso Fresco has a lower fat level, making it suitable for a balanced diet.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Fresh milk used to make the cheese may retain live cultures that benefit gut health.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy or lactose may react to Queso Fresco.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The cheese is often salted; those limiting sodium should monitor intake.

items.title: Perishable product
items.content: High moisture makes Queso Fresco quick to spoil; keep it refrigerated and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Queso Fresco can be diced, crumbled into salads, added to tacos, burritos, soups, and casseroles. It is commonly served with lime, fresh cilantro, and chili. The cheese pairs well with avocado, tomatoes, and corn.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Queso Fresco in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1–4 °C. It can be frozen, but the texture will change. Discard any cheese with off‑odors or mold.

shrimp-and-noodles-with-mushroom-sauce.title: Shrimp and Noodles with Mushroom Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp and noodles with mushroom sauce is a dish that combines seafood, pasta, and a savory mushroom cream sauce. The shrimp are usually sautéed until lightly golden, while the noodles (egg or wheat) are cooked al dente. The mushroom sauce adds a smooth, slightly creamy flavor with earthy undertones.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp are a high‑protein, low‑calorie seafood, making them popular in health‑focused diets.
Mushrooms naturally contain vitamin D when exposed to ultraviolet light.
The tradition of pairing seafood with noodles originates from Asian cuisines, where the combination is considered harmonious in texture and taste.
A creamy mushroom sauce is often finished with white wine or broth to enhance the mushroom aroma.
The dish can be prepared quickly—typically 20–30 minutes from start to plate.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat dishes, shrimp contain relatively little saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both mushrooms and shrimp supply B‑vitamins such as B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The meal delivers zinc, selenium, and iron, which are important for immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain noodles adds fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Additives in sauces
items.content: Store‑bought mushroom sauces can contain MSG and preservatives that may not suit everyone.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly stored shrimp can harbor bacteria such as Vibrio, so proper refrigeration is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté the shrimp in olive oil until pink, then set aside. Cook the noodles separately until al dente. In the same pan, sauté sliced mushrooms, deglaze with a splash of white wine, add cream, salt, pepper, and herbs (parsley, thyme). Toss the noodles and shrimp into the sauce, heat through for 1–2 minutes. Serve hot, garnished with fresh herbs and a lemon wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh shrimp refrigerated at 0‑2 °C and use within 2 days; cooked noodles store in an airtight container for up to 3 days. The mushroom sauce can be frozen for up to 1 month; thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Snowpeas are young pea pods harvested at the earliest stage of growth. The NS (non‑shelled) version refers to whole, intact pods, and “form” indicates that the pods retain their natural shape. The product is ready to eat after cooking: it keeps a crisp texture, a delicate sweet flavor, and a bright green color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snowpeas belong to the legume family and are close relatives of garden peas and beans.
Pods are picked when they are only 3–5 cm long, which makes them especially tender and sweet.
The NS (non‑shelled) variant is popular in gourmet cuisine for its visual appeal.
Snowpeas are rich in B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and folate.
In Japan they are often served as salads or side dishes with sushi.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Snowpeas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many legumes, snowpeas contain virtually no fat, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The pods contain vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, iron, and magnesium, which support immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Snowpeas raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including snowpeas.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Like other legumes, snowpeas can cause flatulence in sensitive people.

items.title: Requires cooking
items.content: Raw pods contain anti‑nutritional factors and should be cooked before consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook snowpeas in boiling water for 3–5 minutes until tender, then shock in ice water to preserve the bright color. They can be added to salads, soups, stews, used as a side for fish or meat, or incorporated into Asian dishes such as stir‑fries or sushi rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked snowpeas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Raw pods are best kept in a cool, dry place in a ventilated bag, where they stay fresh for about 7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Winter squash (Cucurbita maxima) is a large, dense vegetable with sweet flesh. When cooked with added fat (oil or butter) it becomes tender and aromatic, commonly used in side dishes, casseroles and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Winter squash belongs to the gourd family and is cultivated in temperate climates.
Its flesh is rich in beta‑carotene, a provitamin A compound.
Squash can be stored in a cool place for up to 6 months, making it a key winter staple.
Pumpkin seeds left after cooking are high in zinc and magnesium.
In many cultures it appears in traditional dishes such as American pumpkin pie or Russian pumpkin kasha.

items.title: High in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart function.

items.title: Beneficial fats when cooked
items.content: A modest amount of added oil enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Low natural sugar
items.content: Winter squash has a low glycemic index, useful for blood‑sugar management.

items.title: Squash allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to squash.

items.title: High‑calorie additions
items.content: Excessive fat added during cooking raises the calorie content of the dish.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Squash contains modest oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Winter squash can be roasted, stewed, steamed or boiled. Add a drizzle of olive oil or a pat of butter at the end of cooking to boost flavor. Serve as a side, in soups, stews, or mash it into a puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole squash in a cool, dry, dark place at 0‑10 °C. Once cut or cooked, keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days.
